But you will have to outmaneuver your opponents: devious appliances, each as ambitious and dangerous as you. Let the machinations begin! Power Vacuum is a trick-taking card game with a few treacherous twists. Winning tricks gains you Power, but losing them lets you manipulate it between players. Your secret Agenda card motivates you to prop other players up or bring them down. And suits are visible on card backs! Number of players: 1 - 5 Game duration: 22 mn Complexity: 2 / 5 Play Power Vacuum and 1414 other games online. No download necessary - play directly from your web browser. Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 2 Card Dynamics 3 Turn 4 Manipulating the Control Board 5 Round End 6 Game End Overview Be the first to 40 points Card Dynamics In this trick taking game, a few variations need to be noted Red (Violence) is always the trump suit The suit of a card is shown on the back, so what suits a player holds is always visible to everyone else Brown (Spies) are NOT brown on the back, instead have one of the other suit colours to keep them disguised Turn The first player plays any card they wish, to Lead the trick All other players must follow suit if possible, or play a red trump or brown spy If the Leader plays a Brown Spy, the other players do NOT have to follow suit even if they can If all cards are of the lead suit, or there are no special cards, the player who played the highest lead card wins the trick If at least one card played is the Red Trump, the highest trump card played wins If at least one card played is a Brown Spy, this beats a Red Trump, but does NOT beat lead cards i.e. if no other card is red, brown does NOT win Regardless of how someone wins the trick, they can either take a point token or take a card played that round into their hand, the rest of the played cards are discarded In addition, whoever played the lowest value card regardless of suit can manipulate the control board (note, this can also be the winner e.g. if you lead with a green 1, and opponent plays yellow 7, you have both won and played the lowest value card) Manipulating the Control Board First, Transfer Power by moving a power token between the two points of the cable, the non-allocated wedge is the supply, so either take from the supply to give to the appliance or take from the appliance and put back in the supply. If the cable is between two appliances, and one has no power, there is no choice and you have to transfer from the one with power. Afterwards, choose one end of the cable and move it to a different socket (either an appliance or the supply wedge) Each player has a secret agenda card, depicting two appliances, you are trying to have one appliance with the most power and the other with the least. These cards can be orientated as you like when revealed, so it's your choice which you're aiming to have the most and thus which you're aiming to have the least. You can choose to reveal your agenda at any point in your turn as a free action, this will grant it points at end of round based on cards in hand at that moment (between 5-8) for each correct segment, but you will also have to pick the orientation at that moment too Alternatively, you can not reveal your agenda during round, and instead reveal and orientate it at end of round. However, you must be correct on BOTH halves to score 14 points, whilst revealing during round you have the option to score points when only one OR both segments are correct. [Rating: 1/10] Kind of a mess as a trick-taker. Hands are too small, and everyone can see what suits you have. There was way more to do when you have smaller cards, but the reward for high cards felt nonexistent. What makes this different from Backyardia is all the slooow dithering that goes on when you're the lowest, deciding A to B or vice versa. It's the slowest trick-taker I've ever played, and the tricks don't really matter anyway because of the huge reward from bidding. Yet you represent one of the suits anyway, for some reason?  But as a larger political game, it also seemed disappointing to everyone 

[Rating: 2/10] Cool Material. KS typical nonsense added… Totaly random, Not intuitiv  I don’t like it! Better play CAT in the Box!!!

[Rating: 2/10] A trick-taking game where not all the cards are dealt, where some cards can be saved, and where you can play spy cards regardless of suit. No control whatsoever and therefore a terrible game. I hated it.

[Rating: 2.9/10] Another game that was released without being fully play-tested.  There is a difference between having a cool concept and making a fully competent and internally consistent game.  Somewhere inside this is an amazing trick-taking game, but the designers/developers got to the point of cool idea and just stopped.  What you get out is an unbalanced chaotic mess, which spells disaster for a trick-taking game.  EVERYONE!  Gather round...to make a good trick-taking game you need to offer balance and control.  Then, you can layer the fun theme or twist.  Don't expect the other way around to work just b

[Rating: 3/10] Power Vacuum was a game I purchased on kickstarter and later regretted it even before it released. But I wanted to remain positive and once it arrived I gave it my all multiple times with different groups of people. What came out of it is a game that ultimately made you want to always lose to manipulate the board and then win. There was little to no board discussion, everyone was rather silent / absent within the time of playing, and for a game that lasts roughly 30-45 minutes, to become so detached from the game itself that quickly it really speaks for itself.

[Rating: 3/10] Possibly the worst published trick-taking game I have played. Certainly in the worst five. The trick-taking is nearly irrelevant - it's all about manipulating the power tokens, and there is very little control there.

[Rating: 3.7/10] If two or more players share the same goal (e.g. get white to the top), they are almost certain to achieve that goal, whereas somebody who doesn't share any goals with other players has no chance. Also, the random fact of having trumps and spies is a great way to not only make points this round, but also to collect good cards for the next. So while you can argue that if player A had better cards this round, you may have them next round, that's not fully true, as player A will also have good cards next round - the one that she kept.

[Rating: 4/10] A forgettable trick taking game with a cute theme and artwork. Not enough there though to make it stand out.

[Rating: 4/10] I didn't find enough strategy in either the trick-taking nor the control board in this one. For the trick-taking, the small hands (8 cards), super trump, and lack of bidding are unappealing. Also, the middle cards have no value. The control board actions initially feel fun, but the decision is easy to make (i.e., connect the alliance I want to lose with the one most are incentivized to win) especially when allegiances are revealed early.

[Rating: 4/10] Trick taking with some risks and secret scoring element. Overall not my genre and no need to push the envelope so no reason to continue playing this game.

[Rating: 4/10] With the deluxe components! Likely going up on the tradeblock for someone whose group would appreciate it more.  For us, it was just too much for too little. You have trump, but there are also spies which look like other suits. You want to win tricks, but coming last is just as good many times. You get points for your own power, but you also have an agenda that may or may not care about your own power (and the same goes for everyone else).
